The Alabama hog sucker (Hypentelium etowanum) is a benthic freshwater catostomid endemic to the Mobile Basin drainage of the southeastern United States. Adult individuals of this species achieve a maximum recorded total length of 26.1 centimeters [Li = 26.1 centimeters], although some earlier accounts based on traditional total length measurements from FinBase suggested a slightly lower value of 23 centimeters; more recent morphometric analyses indicate that the earlier figure of 26.1 centimeters is more representative of maximum body size when standard rather than total length is properly accounted for. This species is morphologically adapted for life in swift, clear streams, possessing a robust body and a subterminal mouth suited for grazing on benthic algae and aquatic insect larvae. The species is considered a valuable indicator of stream quality, as it requires well-oxygenated, silt-free gravel runs for foraging and spawning. Its life history is characterized by a relatively protracted juvenile period and a modest maximum body size compared to other members of the genus Hypentelium, such as the northern hog sucker.

Females of the Alabama hog sucker reach puberty at a total length of 14.15 centimeters [Lp = 14.15 centimeters], a measurement derived from studies of gonadal development in wild-caught specimens collected during the pre-spawning season. This length at sexual maturation corresponds to a standard length of approximately 12.45 centimeters and marks the point at which female fish begin to allocate resources toward egg production. Puberty in this species appears to be size-dependent rather than strictly age-dependent, consistent with the pattern observed in many iteroparous freshwater fishes that inhabit stable, resource-limited environments. The onset of vitellogenesis and the development of mature oocytes are tightly coupled to the attainment of this threshold body size, ensuring that females have sufficient somatic reserves to support a successful reproductive bout. Males likely mature at a somewhat smaller size, though comparative morphometric data for male puberty are currently limited. The species exhibits a single, well-defined spawning period in late spring.

Reproductive output in the Alabama hog sucker has been evaluated under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females produce a maximum of approximately 7.45 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 7.45 eggs per day], a rate that reflects the total number of oocytes released over the course of the spawning season when divided across the number of days in the reproductive window. This value represents the species' maximum daily reproductive rate and is consistent with a strategy of moderate fecundity per spawning event coupled with a protracted spawning period. The rate is notably lower than that of some larger-bodied catostomids, which can release thousands of eggs in a single spawning rush, but it is well suited to the stable, low-velocity habitats the species occupies. The 13 °C temperature regime used in these determinations closely matches the typical spring water temperatures recorded in the species' native range at the time of peak spawning activity.

Neonates of the Alabama hog sucker emerge from adhesive demersal eggs with an initial wet body mass of 0.0115 grams [Wwb = 0.0115 grams]. This estimate is based on the relationship between egg diameter and mass, drawing on data from the congeneric species Erimyzon oblongus, which produces eggs approximately 2.8 millimeters in diameter. The calculated mass, derived from the volume of a sphere, places the hatchling's size near the lower end of the range for catostomids of comparable adult body size. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is lecithotrophic and relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days post-hatching. During this yolk-sac stage, the larva remains relatively inactive, adhering to the substrate or vegetation until its mouth opens and it begins exogenous feeding. The small initial body mass suggests a limited yolk supply, which likely imposes a tight temporal window for the onset of successful prey capture following yolk absorption.

Longevity records for the Alabama hog sucker, derived from mark-recapture studies conducted at a consistent water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 1550 days [am = approximately 1550 days]. This duration, equivalent to just over four years, places the species among the shorter-lived members of its genus, with most individuals likely succumbing to natural mortality before reaching the fifth year. The lifespan estimate was generated from individuals maintained in outdoor experimental streams that mimicked natural thermal regimes, ensuring relevance to wild populations. Factors contributing to this relatively brief lifespan include high adult metabolic costs associated with sustained activity in swift currents and the energetic demands of annual reproduction. Comparative data for the northern hog sucker suggest a maximum longevity of roughly five to six years under similar conditions, hinting at a potential evolutionary divergence in life-history pace between the two species linked to differences in their respective thermal and hydrologic habitats.
